original.target_description: Experiment 3: noun versus verb wording, official-record voter turnout among registered New Jersey voters in the 2009 gubernatorial election; logistic regression condition effect without the premanipulation turnout covariate.

n.sample_role: Participants matched in official New Jersey voter turnout records and retained in the critical condition-effect analysis.
n.exclusions: 350 completed; 293 met screening eligibility; 214 matched in official records. All matched participants retained; potential condition-based outliers were not excluded.

replication.target_description: Gerber, Huber, and Fang published article, single 2015 field experiment: pooled YouGov/SSI registered-voter sample in Kentucky, Louisiana, Mississippi, and Houston; actual general-election turnout from voter files; intent-to-treat comparison of assignment to 10-item noun wording versus verb wording, covariate-adjusted ordinary least squares primary model.

n.sample_role: Participants in the pooled primary turnout intent-to-treat regression; 1579 noun-assigned and 1499 verb-assigned.
n.exclusions: Eligibility screeners preceded randomization (adult registered voters in target locations; SSI valid identifying information). Primary ITT retains assigned participants without requiring completion of all 10 survey items; the 3033 complete-item sample is a separate robustness analysis. No further primary-analysis exclusions are established.
n.location: Published main article p. 934 (article-relative p. 10; combined PDF p. 36), Results, first paragraph; Table 3, Entire Sample, regression estimate of difference (noun minus verb). Eligibility and ITT details: main pp. 932–933 (combined PDF pp. 34–35), Subject recruitment and sample definition, Estimation, footnote 15.

es.metric: ordinary least squares regression coefficient (difference in turnout probability, noun minus verb)
es.location: Article p. 9 (933), Estimation; p. 10 (934), Table 3 Entire Sample / Regression Estimate of Difference and Results first paragraph; supplied PDF pp. 35–36
es.quote:
Our primary specification is an ordinary least squares model regressing a binary indicator
for voting in the 2015 election on assignment to the noun block and pretreatment covariates. ... In the pooled sample, turnout levels are about 0.7 percentage points higher in the
noun condition than in the verb condition (44.5% vs. 43.6%; regression-based treatment effect
estimate 5 0.007; SE 5 0.012; n 5 3078; p 5 0.57, two-tailed).

p.location: Published main article p. 934 (article-relative p. 10; combined PDF p. 36), Results, first paragraph; Table 3, Entire Sample, regression estimate of difference (noun minus verb).

reported_success.quote: We find no evidence that noun wording increases subjects’ turnout.
